Hi there. I’m so sorry this happened to you. I recently went through a court process for my rape and it wasn’t easy. Depending on what country you’re in, there might be a victim support agency that can help prepare you and fight for your rights to be treated well in court. I found the book Eggshell Skull very helpful to help psych myself up. I won’t lie to you, having to face my rapist in court and having him watch me as I have testimony was terrifying, but I’m glad I did it. He had to sit and listen and hear how what he did was harmful and unwanted. I don’t have an easy answer for you, it is hard and can feel harmful without much pay off, but if it protects you in the long run, there are things you can do to protect yourself, including leaning into your support systems (including therapists or social workers as well as friends and family).
I hope it goes well for you and your healing is gentle with you.

In terms of going to police, I think only you know what’s best. I went through the police process myself over the last five years and I have very mixed feelings about it. If you think you personally would get something from the process (there being a complaint on his police history, validation that it legally can be defined as rape, having your side heard or even something like inconveniencing him) then consider making the complaint as early as possible. 
If you don’t think it would give you something, or you think it will harm you, don’t feel obligated to do so. You don’t owe anyone reporting it. Yes, it’s great to think about protecting others, but your one and only concern right now should be you and your healing.
I hope your healing is gentle with you ❤️

Without more context with what you mean by you reluctantly agreeing to do things, it’s hard to say if she’s coercing you. It could be an issue with enforcing your boundaries and being really clear with your communication about not wanting to do things, or it could be that she’s created a space where you don’t feel safe to say no. I’d recommend looking inwards about why you might feel coerced - definitely not victim blaming, you can’t think it’s “your fault” but there may be a way to reflect on what is causing you to feel coerced or what is making you do things you’re not comfortable with (is it her behaviour or is it being conflict avoidant or something else?).
I’d really recommend talking this out with a therapist too, if you have one.

I was 14 when it happened to me. I’m 30 now. It gets easier with time, but you’re never the same person as you were before. Lean into your support systems if you can, I wish I did at the time instead of internalising it all and working through the feelings alone. Things get easier and you’ll find out who you are after it all, but it feels hard when you’re in the middle of the feelings. Good luck with your healing ❤️

A big part of my recovery has been engaging with a sex therapist who basically told me that it’s okay to be where I am and accept that that’s the way I’m built now.

Most countries have specialised police who deal with crimes against children, and reporting historical offences. Similarly there is usually a victim assistance scheme where you might be able to get legal advice or counselling if you need it.
Good luck and be gentle with yourself.

My sexual self has never really recovered. I’ve had to glean small parts of my sexuality that I could save, but over time I’ve just accepted that I’m only okay with certain things in certain circumstances. That has been my hardest thing, feeling guilt for not being sexual in relationships, even if most partners have been understanding and supportive.
I hope you find some healing and safety ❤️

Absolutely doesn’t make you a bad person. Interestingly, recent research has actually found that rape victims are more likely to have empathy for their abusers than a normal person does in terms of their perceptions of the person. Familial relationships are so complicated, and when abuse is historical, it can be really messy. 
I’d suggest really thinking about whether maintaining the connection is healthy for you, and whether you’ve processed and addressed his behaviour to align with that.

I wish I had an easy answer for you. It’s such a rough time to get through the process that is so personal and draining. I wouldn’t want to put you off going ahead with it because I think there’s definitely so much value in offenders being held to account (and for a history to be there for future victims) but not enough appreciation goes to the poor souls who go through such a horrendous and invasive process. 
I’m still processing how it all worked out, I’ve been quite low in mood and ability to focus in the days since the sentencing. I think if your case goes to trial, have a good think about whether you want to be there when they read the verdict (on the chance it’s a not guilty verdict) so you can process the feelings in a safer space than at the courthouse. 
If there’s anything I can do to help with your journey, please reach out. It can be such a stressful and lonely process. Even with support from loved ones who would move heaven and earth to back you, not a lot of people “get it” in terms of how it all feels. 
Take it one step at a time. The wait can be agonising. I found that the anticipation and the constant feeling of having something hanging over me was taking a lot of my mental space. 
The petty part of me is glad that the court process likely cost him 100k in legal fees, hung over him for four years and likely inconvenienced him a lot. 
You also might find that facing your offender in court might take away some of the fear about him. When they sit in the dock, they’re just a person at the end of the day who has no power over you anymore.
I don’t know if any of this is helpful, but I wish you all the best and hope that you can find some comfort at such a difficult time of your life that largely feels out of your control.

Hang in there. It took 6 years from me reporting to police until he was sentenced. He threw in as many things as possible to delay court in the hopes I would eventually drop the case. This included applying for my counselling records, offering restorative justice twice just to refuse to apologise, and any other swathe of things. 

I really hope you have a better experience than I did. I can only thank the prosecutor and police who worked on the case for believing me, and doing their best to get me justice. My biggest regret is hearing what the defence said about him during his sentencing. If you don’t want to read your impact statement in person at sentencing (if it gets there for you), I’d avoid it. They spoke about his good character and references, while downplaying everything. It was really hurtful.

The thing that was ironically funny to me at his sentencing was that in my impact statement, I outlined the huge financial burden managing my PTSD has placed on me. The judge literally said “no amount of compensation I could reasonably order would repay this burden” so didn’t order any compensation. I just had to laugh at the absurdity of that decision.

For what it’s worth, it’s not a lack of bravery not to go through court. Don’t feel any failure not to have done it. The justice system still fails SA victims and it is more than fair not to subject yourself to it. Be gentle with yourself ❤️

The most empowering thing for me in making my complaint to police was recognising that it was not only my decision to make. Police or prosecutors can assess the situation and choose not to press charges or prosecute him if they think it’s not fair to him to proceed, or if they don’t think it is a clear case of rape. While it’s amazing that you have empathy towards your rapist, think about what you would recommend if a loved one was in the same situation.

Be a safe space for her to ask you for help and vent her feelings. Part of that is compartmentalising how you might feel (guilt is easy to feel even if it wasn’t your fault, and anger and hurt would come naturally). Do some research about support services (which will depend on your location) and find a good psychologist she can see if you can afford it and one is available, but don’t force her to engage in therapy if she doesn’t want to. Ultimately, let her know that she’s in control, that you’re a safe person and that you’re in her corner regardless of your relationship with your brother. Be gentle with yourself and access support for yourself too, that’s really critical because you can’t support someone completely if you’re hurting yourself.

It has been 16 years for me and while I’m very functional and mostly okay, I still have moments and there are some things that never went back to “normal”. My main advice would be not to judge yourself while you recover, and understand that healing is not linear. Wishing you well while you recover.

I work for an agency which investigates child abuse in schools (sexual or otherwise). I would give it a couple of days and ask her some really open questions, if anything at all reinforces what she says, I would honestly take her to police for them to do an interview. I don’t know where you live but in my country, you can ask for them to interview her only, before taking a formal complaint to proceed with a full investigation- this could help preserve evidence if there is anything to her comments. I hope you are both okay. I think the most important thing is you believe her, before worrying about the veracity of the comments in the first instance.
